📄 President Pezeshkian urges unity, focus on public needs amid economic war

📌 Tehran, IRNA – Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian has urged government officials to avoid divisive disputes and mobilize all available resources to address people’s problems, saying national unity could turn economic hardship into an opportunity to tackle long-standing issues.

Speaking at a cabinet meeting on Wednesday, Pezeshkian stressed the importance of cooperation and clearly defined responsibilities in neighborhood-based initiatives led by mosques to address local needs and strengthen social trust.
​
He called for greater involvement of experts, philanthropists and volunteer groups, with services and responsibilities coordinated to ensure effective assistance.
​
The president also highlighted efforts to curb excessive fuel consumption and smuggling. He said authorities had reviewed vulnerabilities across relevant agencies, including the oil, roads and urban development, agriculture, and industry, mining and trade ministries. As part of the measures, 600,000 diesel fuel cards without valid identification had been deactivated, he noted.
​
Pezeshkian said coordinated efforts had eliminated the need to import gasoline, which would otherwise have cost the country $8 billion. He added that reconstruction of damaged industries, roads, bridges and electricity and gas facilities was continuing despite wartime operations.
​
He attributed the progress to the efforts of public employees, managers and citizens, stressing that national cohesion and sustained work were essential to overcoming challenges.
​
President’s aide stresses social cohesion amid war
​
The President’s social affairs aide Ali Rabiei made similar comments on Wednesday evening at a meeting in Isfahan.
​
Rabiei said that Iran needs stronger social cohesion than ever as it faces war and crisis, arguing that the enemy is actively seeking to fuel public discontent and drive people toward protests.
​
He stressed the need for greater public awareness and stronger engagement between civil society institutions and the public.

🇺🇸💣Trump Weighs ‘Mother of All Bombs’ for Iran—But It’s More Show Than Substance in Reality.

➡️According to CNN, Washington is weighing its next move against Tehran, US military planners have drafted fresh strike options targeting Iranian nuclear sites and energy infrastructure. Among the weapons on the table? The GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast—better known as the “Mother of All Bombs” (MOAB).

➡️While dropping America’s largest non-nuclear weapon would signal a massive escalation, military insiders are raising major red flags over whether the bomb can actually deliver on President Donald Trump’s strategic goals.

🔸Big Blast, Limited Impact.
Despite its terrifying reputation, military experts and officials familiar with internal planning discussions warn that the 21,600-pound monster is largely the wrong tool for the job.

🔸It Doesn't Dig Deep: Despite its size, the MOAB is an air-burst weapon designed for surface clearance, not fortified underground targets. "The MOAB is a massive information operation type weapon that is great for huge area clearance, but not much else," one source familiar with military planning told CNN. "It is definitely not designed as a deep penetration warhead."

🔸Surface-Level Havoc: While the bomb creates a terrifying blast wave, its destructive power remains mostly on the surface—meaning heavily fortified or deeply buried Iranian nuclear facilities would likely survive the strike.

🔸High Civilian Risk: The bomb’s massive blast radius poses a severe risk of collateral damage, especially if dropped near Iran's energy infrastructure situated near populated, non-military areas which of course Washington doesn't care about.

➡️If the White House decides to authorize the weapon, officials acknowledge the move would be aimed more at psychological shock than tactical necessity. With Tehran dug in and resisting diplomatic pressure, deploying the MOAB offers a high-profile flex short of launching full-scale combat operations.

➡️Yet, US officials privately concede that even a shock-and-awe moment with the MOAB is unlikely to force Iran’s capitulation or tilt the course of the conflict in a meaningful way—leaving critical questions about whether the risky escalation is worth the military trade-off.
